title: Πρόμος
titleEn: Hector Calls for a Champion — Iliad 7.1–91
about: Hector and Alexander come out of the gates to their weary army like a wind to tired rowers, and the brothers and Glaucus between them kill three Achaeans: Menesthius, Eioneus and Iphinous. Athena sees it and goes down from Olympus; Apollo rises from Pergamus to meet her, and they meet at the oak. He asks whether she means to give the Danaans a victory, proposes that they stop the fighting for the day, and suggests rousing Hector to challenge a single Achaean; she agrees. Helenus, Priam’s son, grasps the gods’ plan and tells his brother Hector to sit both armies down and challenge the best of the Achaeans, since it is not yet his fate to die. Hector holds back the Trojan lines and Agamemnon seats the Achaeans; Athena and Apollo settle on Zeus’s oak like vultures to watch. Hector then calls on the Achaeans for a champion and sets the terms: the winner strips the dead man’s armour, the body goes back for burial, and a tomb on the Hellespont will keep the name of the man who killed him.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν πυλέων ἐξέσσυτο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ,
τῷ δ’ ἅμ’ Ἀλέξανδρος κί’ ἀδελφεός·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, from the gates rushed out glorious Hector,
and with him went Alexander, his brother;
sentences.i: So saying, glorious Hector rushed out from the gates, and his brother Alexander went with him;
sentences.n: Hector leaves the city for the fighting, with Paris at his side. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes his reply to Paris at the end of the last part. ἐξέσσυτο is the aorist of ἐκσεύομαι ‘rush out’, and πυλέων is the epic genitive plural of πύλαι ‘gates’; φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is Hector’s stock epithet, translated each time. κί’ is the elided κίε, an unaugmented past tense of κίω ‘go’, and ἀδελφεός is the epic form of ἀδελφός ‘brother’. Ἀλέξανδρος is the other name of Paris.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα θυμῷ
ἀμφότεροι μέμασαν πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and in spirit
both were eager to wage war and to fight.
sentences.i: and in spirit both were eager to wage war and to fight.
sentences.n: The sentence runs on across the line end: the two brothers are eager for battle. ἐν δ’ ἄρα θυμῷ ‘and in spirit’ says where the eagerness lay. μέμασαν is a past plural of the old perfect μέμαα ‘be eager’. πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι ‘to wage war and to fight’ is a pair of infinitives joined by the epic ἠδέ ‘and’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ θεὸς ναύτῃσιν ἐελδομένοισιν ἔδωκεν
οὖρον, ἐπεί κε κάμωσιν ἐϋξέστῃς ἐλάτῃσι
πόντον ἐλαύνοντες, καμάτῳ δ’ ὑπὸ γυῖα λέλυνται,
ὣς ἄρα τὼ Τρώεσσιν ἐελδομένοισι φανήτην.
sentences.l:
As a god to sailors longing has given
a fair wind, when they have grown weary with well-polished fir-oars
driving the open-sea, and beneath weariness their limbs are loosened,
so then the two to the Trojans longing appeared.
sentences.i: As a god gives a fair wind to sailors who long for it, when they have grown weary driving the sea with well-polished fir-oars and their limbs are loosened under the weariness, so the two appeared to the Trojans, who longed for them.
sentences.n: A simile: the brothers’ arrival is like the wind that comes to rowers worn out at the oars. ὡς δὲ … ὣς ἄρα ‘as … so’ opens and closes it, and ἐελδομένοισιν (sailors) and ἐελδομένοισι (Trojans) are the same participle, dative plural of ἐέλδομαι ‘long for’, which binds the halves. ἔδωκεν is an aorist for what happens whenever it happens, so English says ‘gives’; ἐπεί κε κάμωσιν is ‘when they have grown weary’ (aorist subjunctive). ἐλάτῃσι is the dative plural of ἐλάτη, the fir and so the oar of fir. λέλυνται, perfect passive, ‘are loosened’, is the verb of λύντο at 12 and 16. τὼ is the dual ‘the two’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἑλέτην ὃ μὲν υἱὸν Ἀρηϊθόοιο ἄνακτος
Ἄρνῃ ναιετάοντα Μενέσθιον, ὃν κορυνήτης
γείνατ’ Ἀρηΐθοος καὶ Φυλομέδουσα βοῶπις·
sentences.i: There the two killed, the one Menesthius, the son of the lord Areithous, who lived in Arne, whom Areithous the club-wielder and ox-eyed Phylomedusa had begotten;
sentences.n: Each brother makes a kill. ἔνθ’ ἑλέτην ‘there the two took’: ἑλέτην is a dual aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, which of a man in battle means ‘slay’. ὃ μὲν ‘the one’ is answered by Ἕκτωρ δ’ in line 11, so he is Alexander. His victim is Μενέσθιον, son of Ἀρηϊθόοιο ἄνακτος ‘Areithous the lord’ (epic genitive -οιο), Ἄρνῃ ναιετάοντα ‘dwelling in Arne’. κορυνήτης is ‘club-wielder’, from κορύνη ‘club’. γείνατ’ is γείνατο, an unaugmented aorist ‘begot’, with Areithous and Φυλομέδουσα, βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’, as joint subject.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ Ἠϊονῆα βάλ’ ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι
αὐχέν’ ὑπὸ στεφάνης εὐχάλκου, λύντο δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.l:
And Hector Eioneus struck with his sharp spear
in the neck beneath the well-bronzed rim, and his limbs were loosened.
sentences.i: And Hector struck Eioneus with his sharp spear in the neck, under the rim of fine bronze, and his limbs gave way.
sentences.n: Hector’s kill is a blow to the neck. βάλ’ is βάλε, an unaugmented aorist ‘struck’, with ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι ‘a sharp spear’ in the dative of the instrument; αὐχέν’ is the accusative of αὐχήν ‘neck’, the part struck. στεφάνη is a ring or rim, and ὑπὸ στεφάνης εὐχάλκου ‘beneath the well-bronzed rim’ is taken to be the helmet’s rim; εὔχαλκος means ‘of good bronze’. λύντο is an unaugmented aorist of λύω with passive sense (middle in form): λύντο δὲ γυῖα ‘and his limbs were loosened’ is the formula for a man’s death, and returns at 16 translated the same.

sentences.t:
Γλαῦκος δ’ Ἱππολόχοιο πάϊς Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀνδρῶν
Ἰφίνοον βάλε δουρὶ κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην
Δεξιάδην ἵππων ἐπιάλμενον ὠκειάων
ὦμον·
sentences.l:
And Glaucus, Hippolochus’ son, leader of the Lycian men,
Iphinous struck with his spear in strong battle,
Dexiades, leaping upon swift horses,
in the shoulder;
sentences.i: And Glaucus, the son of Hippolochus, leader of the Lycian men, struck Iphinous Dexiades with his spear in strong battle, in the shoulder, as he leapt up onto his swift horses;
sentences.n: Glaucus makes the third kill. Ἱππολόχοιο πάϊς ‘son of Hippolochus’ has the epic genitive -οιο and πάϊς for παῖς; Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀνδρῶν ‘leader of the Lycian men’ is his title. Δεξιάδην is a patronymic like Ἀτρεΐδης (‘son of …’), kept as a name because the father is not named in this part. κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην ‘in strong battle’ is a stock phrase. ἐπιάλμενον is the aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι ‘leap upon’, taking the genitive ἵππων; ὠκειάων is a feminine genitive plural of ὠκύς ‘swift’. ὦμον ‘in the shoulder’ is the part struck, held to the unit’s end.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐξ ἵππων χαμάδις πέσε, λύντο δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.l: and he from the horses to the ground fell, and his limbs were loosened.
sentences.i: and he fell from the horses to the ground, and his limbs gave way.
sentences.n: The death. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ takes up the wounded man again: the article is a pronoun. χαμάδις ‘to the ground’ is an adverb of motion (compare χαμαί ‘on the ground’), and πέσε is an unaugmented aorist of πίπτω ‘fall’. The second half of the line is the formula already used at 12: λύντο δὲ γυῖα ‘and his limbs were loosened’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
Ἀργείους ὀλέκοντας ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ,
βῆ ῥα κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀΐξασα
Ἴλιον εἰς ἱερήν·
sentences.l:
And when, then, she noticed them, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
the Argives destroying in strong battle,
she went then down from the peaks of Olympus, darting,
to sacred Ilium;
sentences.i: And when the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, saw them destroying the Argives in strong battle, she went darting down from the peaks of Olympus to sacred Ilium;
sentences.n: Athena sees the Achaeans losing and comes down from Olympus. τοὺς ‘them’ are the Trojans, whose kills have just been told, and ὀλέκοντας ‘destroying’ agrees with it, with Ἀργείους as its object. The first line is 5.711 with Athena for Hera, and the second is word for word 5.712. βῆ is the unaugmented ἔβη ‘she went’, κατά with the genitive means ‘down from’, and ἀΐξασα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. Ἴλιον εἰς ἱερήν is ‘to sacred Ilium’; the ano teleia closes the unit in the middle of line 20.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ ἀντίος ὄρνυτ’ Ἀπόλλων
Περγάμου ἐκκατιδών, Τρώεσσι δὲ βούλετο νίκην·
sentences.l:
and to meet her rose Apollo,
looking down from Pergamus, and wished victory for the Trojans;
sentences.i: and Apollo, looking down from Pergamus, rose up to meet her; he wished victory for the Trojans;
sentences.n: Apollo has been watching from Troy’s citadel. τῇ is the dative ‘her’ (the article as a pronoun), and ἀντίος ‘face to face, to meet’ takes it; ὄρνυτ’ is the elided ὄρνυτο, an unaugmented imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rose up’. Περγάμου ἐκκατιδών ‘looking down from Pergamus’ is one word for ‘looking down out of’, with the genitive of the place; Pergamus is the high citadel of Troy. βούλετο is an imperfect ‘was wishing’ and takes νίκην ‘victory’ directly, with Τρώεσσι ‘for the Trojans’ in the dative.

sentences.t: ἀλλήλοισι δὲ τώ γε συναντέσθην παρὰ φηγῷ.
sentences.l: And with one another the two of them met beside the oak.
sentences.i: The two met each other beside the oak.
sentences.n: The two gods meet. ἀλλήλοισι ‘one another’ goes with συναντέσθην ‘the two met’, a dual past tense of συναντάω, middle in form; τώ is the dual of the article, ‘those two’, with γε. φηγῷ is the dative of φηγός ‘oak’, and παρά with the dative means ‘beside’. The Greek has no article; ‘the oak’ is the one on which the two gods will perch (60).

sentences.t: τὴν πρότερος προσέειπεν ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: Her first addressed the lord, the son of Zeus, Apollo:
sentences.i: Lord Apollo, the son of Zeus, spoke to her first:
sentences.n: Apollo speaks first, and his speech runs to line 32. τὴν is ‘her’ (the article as a pronoun), and προσέειπεν is the epic aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’; πρότερος is the comparative ‘first of the two’, agreeing with the subject. ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων ‘the lord, the son of Zeus, Apollo’ fills out the line as a name-and-title phrase and is translated the same way each time. The speech itself begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
τίπτε σὺ δ’ αὖ μεμαυῖα Διὸς θύγατερ μεγάλοιο
ἦλθες ἀπ’ Οὐλύμποιο, μέγας δέ σε θυμὸς ἀνῆκεν;
sentences.l:
“Why ever, and you again, eager, daughter of great Zeus,
have you come from Olympus, and has your great spirit sent you up?
sentences.i: “Why, you again, daughter of great Zeus, so eager, have you come from Olympus? Has your great spirit urged you on?
sentences.n: Apollo’s speech opens with a reproach. τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’, and σὺ δ’ αὖ ‘and you again’ turns on Athena (αὖ goes with σύ, not with ἦλθες). μεμαυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of μέμαα ‘be eager’, and Διὸς θύγατερ μεγάλοιο ‘daughter of great Zeus’ is a vocative with the epic genitive -οιο. ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘send up, urge on’; its subject is μέγας θυμός ‘a great spirit’, her own impulse, and σε is its object.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἵνα δὴ Δαναοῖσι μάχης ἑτεραλκέα νίκην
δῷς;
sentences.l:
Is it, then, in order that to the Danaans a victory in battle, other-strengthening,
you may give?
sentences.i: Is it in order that you may give the Danaans a victory in battle that turns the fight to the other side?
sentences.n: He asks what she is after. ἦ ἵνα δή is ‘is it in order that …?’; ἵνα takes the aorist subjunctive δῷς ‘you may give’, which stands at the start of the next line. ἑτεραλκέα νίκην ‘a victory turning the fight to the other side’: ἑτεραλκής is built on ἕτερος ‘the other’ and ἀλκή ‘strength’ and is glossed ‘giving strength to the other side’; here it shifts the battle’s strength to the Danaans. μάχης ‘of the battle’ goes with νίκην. ‘Danaans’ is another of the poet’s names for the army.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ οὔ τι Τρῶας ἀπολλυμένους ἐλεαίρεις.
sentences.l: since not at all the Trojans perishing do you pity.
sentences.i: since you have no pity at all for the Trojans as they perish.
sentences.n: He gives his reason for suspecting her. ἐπεί ‘since’ looks back to the question: she must want that, because she has no pity for the Trojans. οὔ τι is ‘not at all’; ἀπολλυμένους is the present middle participle of ἀπόλλυμι, ‘perishing’, agreeing with Τρῶας; ἐλεαίρεις is an epic form of ἐλεαίρω ‘pity’ and takes the accusative. The unit begins in the middle of line 27, after the question mark.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ εἴ μοί τι πίθοιο τό κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη·
sentences.l: But if you would obey me at all, that would be much better:
sentences.i: But if you would take my advice at all, that would be far better:
sentences.n: He turns from reproach to advice. εἴ … πίθοιο ‘if you would obey’ is a mild condition: πίθοιο is the aorist optative of πείθομαι, with the dative μοι ‘me’, and τό κεν … εἴη ‘that would be’ is its answer, κεν giving the sense of ‘would’. κέρδιον is the comparative ‘better, more advantageous’, here with πολύ ‘much’. The line occurs in the Odyssey also, and the English is the same.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν παύσωμεν πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα
σήμερον·
sentences.l:
Now, for the present, let us stop the war and the fighting
today;
sentences.i: For now let us stop the war and the fighting for today;
sentences.n: His advice is a pause. νῦν μέν ‘now, for the present’ is answered by ὕστερον ‘later’ in the next unit. παύσωμεν is the aorist subjunctive of παύω ‘stop’, used as an exhortation, ‘let us stop’, and it takes two objects, πόλεμον ‘war’ and δηϊοτῆτα ‘fighting’, near-synonyms. σήμερον ‘today’ closes the unit in the middle of line 30, with an ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὕστερον αὖτε μαχήσοντ’ εἰς ὅ κε τέκμωρ
Ἰλίου εὕρωσιν, ἐπεὶ ὣς φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ
ὑμῖν ἀθανάτῃσι, διαπραθέειν τόδε ἄστυ.
sentences.l:
later again they will fight, until an end
of Ilios they find, since so it has been dear to the spirit
of you immortal ones, to sack through and through this town.”
sentences.i: Later they will fight again, until they find an end for Ilios, since it has so pleased the spirit of you immortals to sack this town.”
sentences.n: He says what follows the pause: the fighting resumes until the town’s end is reached, because the goddesses wish it. μαχήσοντ’ is the elided μαχήσονται, future ‘they will fight’. εἰς ὅ κε … εὕρωσιν ‘until they find’ takes the aorist subjunctive; τέκμωρ is a fixed end (at 1.526 the same word is the ‘sign’ of Zeus’s nod). ὑμῖν is plural and ἀθανάτῃσι feminine, ‘you immortal ones’: Apollo speaks to Athena but includes other goddesses, whom he does not name. φίλον ἔπλετο is ‘has been dear’, with θυμῷ ‘to the spirit’ and the dative ὑμῖν naming whose spirit it is (‘to your spirit’). διαπραθέειν is the epic infinitive of διαπέρθω ‘sack through and through’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Athena answers. τὸν is ‘him’ (the article as a pronoun), and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the reply; προσέειπε is the epic aorist ‘addressed’. The line is a formula, found already at 1.206, and the English is the same each time. γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ is Athena’s stock epithet; it is built on γλαυκός ‘gleaming’, and what it means of an eye is disputed.

sentences.t: ὧδ’ ἔστω ἑκάεργε·
sentences.l: “Thus let it be, far-working one;
sentences.i: “Let it be so, you who work from afar;
sentences.n: Athena agrees. ὧδ’ ἔστω ‘so let it be’ is the third-person imperative of εἰμί. ἑκάεργε is the vocative of ἑκάεργος, an epithet of Apollo whose meaning is disputed: ‘far-working’ is one guess and ‘far-shooting’ another, and the English keeps ‘far-working’ without deciding. The ano teleia closes her agreement, and her reason follows.

sentences.t:
τὰ γὰρ φρονέουσα καὶ αὐτὴ
ἦλθον ἀπ’ Οὐλύμποιο μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
for these things thinking, I myself too
came from Olympus among the Trojans and Achaeans.
sentences.i: for I too, with these same thoughts, came from Olympus among the Trojans and Achaeans.
sentences.n: She gives her reason: she came with the same thought. τὰ is ‘these things’ (the article as a demonstrative) and φρονέουσα is the participle of φρονέω ‘think, have in mind’, uncontracted in the epic way (Attic φρονοῦσα); καὶ αὐτή ‘I myself too’ says that she shares Apollo’s thought. ἦλθον is the aorist ‘I came’, ἀπ’ Οὐλύμποιο has the epic genitive -οιο, and μετά with the accusative means ‘among’, ‘into the midst of’, with Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς, the two armies together.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε πῶς μέμονας πόλεμον καταπαυσέμεν ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.l: But come, how are you minded to stop the war of men?”
sentences.i: But come, how do you mean to put a stop to the war of men?”
sentences.n: Her question hands the plan back to him. ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’ is a stock turn, and πῶς ‘how’ goes with μέμονας, a perfect of an old verb with the force of a present, ‘you are minded, you intend’. καταπαυσέμεν is an epic future infinitive in -σέμεν of καταπαύω ‘put an end to’. πόλεμον … ἀνδρῶν ‘the war of men’ uses the genitive for the men who fight it.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the lord, the son of Zeus, Apollo:
sentences.i: Then lord Apollo, the son of Zeus, spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: Apollo replies. The line is the reply formula: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ‘and her in turn he addressed’, with αὖτε ‘in turn’ marking the answer and the name-and-title phrase ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων as in line 23, translated the same way.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορος ὄρσωμεν κρατερὸν μένος ἱπποδάμοιο,
ἤν τινά που Δαναῶν προκαλέσσεται οἰόθεν οἶος
ἀντίβιον μαχέσασθαι ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι,
sentences.i: “Let us rouse the strong might of Hector, tamer of horses, to see if he will challenge some one of the Danaans, all alone, to fight him in open opposition, in fearsome fighting,
sentences.n: Apollo’s plan is to stir Hector into challenging a single Achaean. ὄρσωμεν is the aorist subjunctive of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘let us rouse’; μένος is fighting might, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘horse-taming’, his stock epithet, agrees with Ἕκτορος. ἤν is εἰ ἄν ‘if’, with που ‘perhaps’ and the aorist subjunctive προκαλέσσεται of προκαλέω (middle) ‘challenge’. οἰόθεν οἶος ‘singly, alone’ is two words for one idea. The third line is the line of 3.20, where Alexander made the same challenge.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ κ’ ἀγασσάμενοι χαλκοκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
οἶον ἐπόρσειαν πολεμίζειν Ἕκτορι δίῳ.
sentences.l:
and they, feeling indignation, the bronze-greaved Achaeans,
a single man might rouse to fight with heavenly Hector.”
sentences.i: and the bronze-greaved Achaeans, feeling indignation, might rouse a single man to fight with heavenly Hector.”
sentences.n: He expects the Achaeans to answer with one champion. κε with the optative ἐπόρσειαν (aorist of ἐπόρνυμι ‘rouse up against’) makes it a possibility, ‘might rouse’. ἀγασσάμενοι is the aorist participle of ἀγάομαι, which can mean ‘wonder at’ and also ‘be indignant at’; after a challenge the second sense fits better, and the English follows it, though the choice is a judgment from the context. χαλκοκνήμιδες ‘bronze-greaved’ matches ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’, both from κνημίς ‘greave’. οἶον ‘a single man’ is the object of the infinitive πολεμίζειν, with Ἕκτορι δίῳ ‘heavenly Hector’ in the dative; δῖος is his stock epithet. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
τῶν δ’ Ἕλενος Πριάμοιο φίλος παῖς σύνθετο θυμῷ
βουλήν, ἥ ῥα θεοῖσιν ἐφήνδανε μητιόωσι·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, did not disobey. Helenus, Priam’s dear son, grasped in his spirit the plan that pleased the gods in their devising;
sentences.n: Athena accepts the plan. ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Apollo’s speech; ἔφατ’ is the elided, unaugmented ἔφατο. ἀπίθησε is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’, and οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘and did not disobey’ is the formula for consent. Helenus, a son of Priam and so Hector’s brother, takes in what the gods have planned. τῶν δ’ ‘and of them’ (the article as a pronoun) means the two gods, whose plan it is, and Πριάμοιο φίλος παῖς is ‘Priam’s dear son’, with the epic genitive -οιο. σύνθετο is the aorist middle of συντίθημι ‘put together’, so ‘put together in his spirit’ is ‘understood’, and its object is βουλήν ‘plan’. ἥ ῥα … ἐφήνδανε is a relative clause, ‘which pleased’, with ἐφήνδανε an imperfect of ἐφανδάνω ‘be pleasing’, and θεοῖσιν … μητιόωσι ‘to the gods devising’ in the dative; μητιόωσι is the uncontracted dative plural participle of μητιάω ‘devise’.

sentences.t: στῆ δὲ παρ’ Ἕκτορ’ ἰὼν καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and he stood beside Hector, going, and to him a word he spoke:
sentences.i: He went up to Hector, stood beside him, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: Helenus approaches Hector. στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, intransitive, ‘he stood’; παρ’ Ἕκτορ’ is παρά with the accusative, ‘beside Hector’, and ἰών ‘going’ adds that he came up to him. καί μιν … ἔειπεν is a stock way of introducing speech: μιν is ‘him’, πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν ‘spoke a word to’, and ἔειπεν is the epic form of the aorist εἶπεν.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ υἱὲ Πριάμοιο Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντε
ἦ ῥά νύ μοί τι πίθοιο, κασίγνητος δέ τοί εἰμι·
sentences.l:
“Hector, son of Priam, to Zeus in cunning equal,
truly now, would you obey me at all? and your brother I am:
sentences.i: “Hector, son of Priam, the equal of Zeus in cunning, would you now take my advice at all? I am your brother:
sentences.n: Helenus speaks as a brother. Ἕκτορ υἱὲ Πριάμοιο is the address, followed by Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντε ‘equal to Zeus in cunning’: ἀτάλαντε is the vocative of ἀτάλαντος ‘equal in weight’, μῆτιν the accusative of respect, ‘in cunning’ (μῆτις is ‘cunning’ throughout), and Διί the dative ‘to Zeus’. ἦ ῥά νυ is ‘truly now’, and πίθοιο is the aorist optative of πείθομαι with μοι, ‘would you obey me’, a polite request; τι is ‘at all’. κασίγνητος δέ τοί εἰμι ‘and I am your brother’: τοί is the dative σοι ‘to you’, and the clause gives the reason for listening.

sentences.t:
ἄλλους μὲν κάθισον Τρῶας καὶ πάντας Ἀχαιούς,
αὐτὸς δὲ προκάλεσσαι Ἀχαιῶν ὅς τις ἄριστος
ἀντίβιον μαχέσασθαι ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι·
sentences.i: make the others sit down, the Trojans and all the Achaeans, and yourself challenge whoever is best of the Achaeans to fight you in open opposition, in fearsome fighting;
sentences.n: His advice has three parts: sit the armies down, challenge the best Achaean, and fight him in single combat. The first line is word for word 3.68, where Alexander said it to Hector, and the English is nearly the same (‘all’ is not in the Greek here); the last is the line already used at 40. κάθισον is the aorist imperative of καθίζω used with an object, ‘make sit’, and προκάλεσσαι the aorist imperative middle of προκαλέω ‘challenge’ (σσ is epic). ὅς τις ἄριστος ‘whoever is best’, with Ἀχαιῶν ‘of the Achaeans’ before it.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πώ τοι μοῖρα θανεῖν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν·
sentences.l: for not yet for you is it fate to die and to meet your doom;
sentences.i: for it is not yet your fate to die and meet your doom;
sentences.n: His reason. οὐ γάρ πώ ‘for not yet’; τοι is the dative σοι ‘to you’, as in line 48. μοῖρα is ‘fate, one’s allotted share’, with no verb, ‘it is fate’, and the infinitives θανεῖν ‘to die’ and ἐπισπεῖν depend on it. ἐπισπεῖν is an aorist infinitive of ἐφέπω ‘follow up, bring upon oneself’, and πότμον ἐπισπεῖν ‘to meet one’s doom’ is a set phrase, πότμος ‘doom’ being one’s fated end.

sentences.t: ὣς γὰρ ἐγὼ ὄπ’ ἄκουσα θεῶν αἰειγενετάων.
sentences.l: for so I heard the voice of the gods, the forever-born.”
sentences.i: for that is what I heard the voice of the everlasting gods say.”
sentences.n: The proof: he has heard the gods. ὣς γάρ ‘for so’ gives the reason, and ὄπ’ is the elided ὄπα, accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’, the object of ἄκουσα, an aorist ‘I heard’ (ἤκουσα without its augment). θεῶν αἰειγενετάων ‘of the gods, the forever-born’ is a stock phrase for the immortals; αἰειγενέτης is built on ‘always’ and the root of γίγνομαι ‘be born’. The Greek says only that he heard the voice, not how. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, Ἕκτωρ δ’ αὖτε χάρη μέγα μῦθον ἀκούσας,
καί ῥ’ ἐς μέσσον ἰὼν Τρώων ἀνέεργε φάλαγγας,
μέσσου δουρὸς ἑλών·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector rejoiced greatly to hear the speech, and going into the middle he held back the Trojan battle-lines, grasping his spear by the middle;
sentences.n: Hector accepts and acts at once. ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Helenus’ speech. χάρη is the unaugmented aorist of χαίρω ‘rejoice’, αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the answer, and μῦθον ἀκούσας ‘the word having heard’ is an aorist participle, like ἑλών ‘having taken’. ἀνέεργε is an unaugmented imperfect of ἀνέργω ‘hold back’. μέσσου δουρὸς ἑλών ‘taking hold of the spear by the middle’: a spear held crosswise by its centre is the gesture that holds the lines back. These lines are nearly word for word 3.76–78 (χάρη for ἐχάρη, οἳ for τοὶ), where Hector does the same, and the English is the same.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἱδρύνθησαν ἅπαντες.
sentences.l: and they were seated, all.
sentences.i: and they all sat down.
sentences.n: The Trojan ranks obey. οἳ is ‘they’ (the Trojans) and ἱδρύνθησαν the aorist passive of ἱδρύω ‘cause to sit’, so ‘were seated’; ἅπαντες ‘all’ is the emphatic form of πάντες. The unit begins in the middle of line 56, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ Ἀγαμέμνων εἷσεν ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l: and down Agamemnon seated the well-greaved Achaeans;
sentences.i: and Agamemnon made the well-greaved Achaeans sit down;
sentences.n: Agamemnon does the same for the Achaeans. κὰδ … εἷσεν is a tmesis, the preverb standing apart from its verb: κάδ is κατά ‘down’ with its τ changed to match the δ that follows. εἷσεν is an aorist of ἵζω in the causative sense ‘make sit, seat’. ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς ‘the well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock epithet and the object.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
ἑζέσθην ὄρνισιν ἐοικότες αἰγυπιοῖσι
φηγῷ ἐφ’ ὑψηλῇ πατρὸς Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
ἀνδράσι τερπόμενοι·
sentences.l:
and down then Athena and silver-bowed Apollo
sat, likened to birds, to vultures,
on the high oak of father Zeus, aegis-bearing,
taking delight in the men;
sentences.i: and Athena and silver-bowed Apollo sat down, like birds, like vultures, on the high oak of father Zeus, aegis-bearing, taking delight in the men;
sentences.n: The two gods take their seats as spectators. κὰδ … ἑζέσθην is κατά split from its verb, with ἑζέσθην a dual past tense (imperfect) of ἕζομαι ‘sit’. ὄρνισιν ἐοικότες αἰγυπιοῖσι ‘like birds, vultures’: αἰγυπιός is the vulture, and ἐοικότες is plural in form though the verb is dual, and masculine for a goddess and a god together. πατρὸς Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο ‘of father Zeus, aegis-bearing’ is the stock title, the meaning of αἰγίοχος being disputed. ἀργυρότοξος ‘silver-bowed’ is Apollo’s epithet. ἀνδράσι τερπόμενοι ‘taking delight in the men’: τέρπομαι takes the dative.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ στίχες εἵατο πυκναὶ
ἀσπίσι καὶ κορύθεσσι καὶ ἔγχεσι πεφρικυῖαι.
sentences.l:
and of them the ranks sat thick,
with shields and with helmets and with spears bristling.
sentences.i: and the ranks of the men sat close-packed, bristling with shields and helmets and spears.
sentences.n: The armies sit in dense ranks. τῶν δέ ‘and of them’ refers back to ἀνδράσι, so ‘their ranks’; στίχες is ‘ranks’, εἵατο the epic past tense of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and πυκναί ‘thick, close-packed’ agrees with στίχες. πεφρικυῖαι is the perfect participle of φρίσσω ‘bristle’, feminine plural with στίχες, and the three datives ἀσπίσι, κορύθεσσι and ἔγχεσι say with what; κορύθεσσι is the epic dative plural of κόρυς ‘helmet’.

sentences.t:
οἵη δὲ Ζεφύροιο ἐχεύατο πόντον ἔπι φρὶξ
ὀρνυμένοιο νέον, μελάνει δέ τε πόντος ὑπ’ αὐτῆς,
τοῖαι ἄρα στίχες εἵατ’ Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε
ἐν πεδίῳ·
sentences.l:
And as the ripple of the West Wind has spread over the open-sea,
rising anew, and the open-sea turns dark beneath it,
of such a kind then sat the ranks of the Achaeans and of the Trojans
in the plain;
sentences.i: As the ripple of the West Wind spreads over the sea when it has newly begun to rise, and the sea darkens beneath it, so the ranks of the Achaeans and Trojans sat in the plain;
sentences.n: A second simile: the ranks sitting close and dark are like a sea roughened by wind. οἵη … τοῖαι ‘of what kind … of such a kind’ frames it. φρίξ is the shiver a wind sends over water; ἐχεύατο, aorist middle of χέω ‘pour, spread’, is used for what happens whenever it happens, so English says ‘spreads’; πόντον ἔπι is ἐπὶ πόντον with the accent thrown back. ὀρνυμένοιο νέον ‘rising anew’ agrees with Ζεφύροιο, the West Wind. μελάνει δέ τε πόντος ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ‘and the sea turns dark beneath it’ has the epic τε of a general truth.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δὲ μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔειπε·
sentences.l: and Hector among both spoke:
sentences.i: and Hector spoke among them both:
sentences.n: Hector begins to speak. This half-line is word for word the second half of 3.85 (which begins with ἐσσυμένως), where he also spoke to both armies, and the English is the same. μετά with the dative means ‘among’, and ἀμφοτέροισιν ‘both’ means both armies, now seated. ἔειπε is the epic form of the aorist εἶπε. The speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: Hector’s speech opens with a formula of address. κέκλυτε is a reduplicated imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ that goes with it. Τρῶες καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί ‘Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans’ names both armies. The first line is word for word 3.86 and the second is a line the Odyssey also has (Odyssey 7.187); the English is the same in each. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive, and θυμός ‘heart’ is what bids him, with ἐνὶ στήθεσσι ‘in my breast’.

sentences.t:
ὅρκια μὲν Κρονίδης ὑψίζυγος οὐκ ἐτέλεσσεν,
ἀλλὰ κακὰ φρονέων τεκμαίρεται ἀμφοτέροισιν
εἰς ὅ κεν ἢ ὑμεῖς Τροίην εὔπυργον ἕλητε
ἢ αὐτοὶ παρὰ νηυσὶ δαμείετε ποντοπόροισιν.
sentences.l:
The oaths, indeed, the son of Cronus, sitting on high, did not fulfil,
but thinking evils he fixes matters for both,
until either you take Troy, the well-towered,
or yourselves beside the ships are subdued, the sea-crossing ones.
sentences.i: The son of Cronus, who sits on high, did not fulfil our oaths, but with evil in his mind he fixes matters for both sides, until either you take well-towered Troy or you are subdued beside your sea-crossing ships.
sentences.n: Hector says Zeus has not made the oaths of the truce good, so the war goes on. ὅρκια ‘oaths’ stands first, μέν looking on to ἀλλά; ἐτέλεσσεν is the aorist of τελέω ‘fulfil’ with doubled σσ. Κρονίδης ὑψίζυγος is Zeus without his name (ὑψίζυγος from ὕψι ‘on high’ and ζυγόν ‘bench, seat’). κακὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking evils’; τεκμαίρεται, from τέκμωρ ‘fixed end’, is ‘fixes’ (as τεκμήραντο at 6.349), its object left to be understood. Τροίην εὔπυργον is ‘well-towered Troy’. δαμείετε is the aorist passive subjunctive of δαμάζω with the epic ending -είετε (Attic δαμῆτε). ὑμεῖς and αὐτοί are the Achaeans.

sentences.t: ὑμῖν δ’ ἐν γὰρ ἔασιν ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν·
sentences.l: for among you there are the best men of the Achaeans all together;
sentences.i: for among you are the best men of the Achaeans all together:
sentences.n: He turns to the Achaeans. ὑμῖν ‘to you’ is now the Achaeans alone, since the best of the Achaeans are among them. ἐν … ἔασιν is a tmesis of ἔνεισιν, ‘are in, are among’, with ἔασιν the epic form of εἰσίν, and γάρ stands late in its clause. ἀριστῆες ‘best men’ is a noun, the chiefs, and Παναχαιῶν is the epic genitive plural of Πανάχαιοι ‘all the Achaeans together’.

sentences.t:
τῶν νῦν ὅν τινα θυμὸς ἐμοὶ μαχέσασθαι ἀνώγει
δεῦρ’ ἴτω ἐκ πάντων πρόμος ἔμμεναι Ἕκτορι δίῳ.
sentences.l:
of these, whomever now his spirit bids to fight with me,
let him come here from among all to be champion against heavenly Hector.
sentences.i: Of these, whichever man his spirit now bids to fight me, let him come here, out of all of them, to be champion against heavenly Hector.
sentences.n: The challenge itself. τῶν ‘of these’ is partitive, the best men just named. ὅν τινα … ἀνώγει ‘whomever … bids’ puts the relative clause first; θυμός is the man’s own spirit, and ἐμοὶ μαχέσασθαι is ‘to fight with me’. ἴτω is the third-person imperative of εἶμι, with δεῦρ’ ‘here’, and ἐκ πάντων is ‘out of all’. πρόμος is ‘the foremost fighter, a champion’, ἔμμεναι the epic infinitive of εἰμί, and Ἕκτορι δίῳ ‘heavenly Hector’ is the dative for the man he is to face: Hector speaks of himself in the third person, with his stock epithet δῖος.

sentences.t: ὧδε δὲ μυθέομαι, Ζεὺς δ’ ἄμμ’ ἐπιμάρτυρος ἔστω·
sentences.l: And thus I speak, and Zeus for us let be witness:
sentences.i: This is what I say, and let Zeus be our witness:
sentences.n: He sets out his terms and calls on Zeus. ὧδε ‘thus’ looks forward to the terms, and μυθέομαι is ‘speak, say’. ἄμμ’ is an elided Aeolic form of ‘us’; the lost vowel does not show whether it is the dative ἄμμι or the accusative ἄμμε, and the English reads it ‘for us’. ἐπιμάρτυρος ‘witness’ is a noun used as predicate, and ἔστω is the imperative ‘let him be’. The ano teleia introduces the terms.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κεν ἐμὲ κεῖνος ἕλῃ ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ,
τεύχεα συλήσας φερέτω κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας,
σῶμα δὲ οἴκαδ’ ἐμὸν δόμεναι πάλιν, ὄφρα πυρός με
Τρῶες καὶ Τρώων ἄλοχοι λελάχωσι θανόντα.
sentences.l:
If that man should take me with the long-pointed bronze,
having stripped my armour let him carry it to the hollow ships,
but my body home to give back, so that of fire me
the Trojans and the wives of the Trojans may give a share, when I am dead.
sentences.i: If that man kills me with his long-pointed bronze, let him strip my armour and carry it to the hollow ships, but let him give my body back home, so that the Trojans and the Trojans’ wives may give me my share of fire when I am dead.
sentences.n: The first condition: if the Achaean wins, he keeps the armour but returns the body. εἰ μέν κεν … ἕλῃ ‘if he should take’ has the aorist subjunctive; αἱρέω ‘take’ of a man in battle means ‘slay’. ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ ‘with long-pointed bronze’: ταναήκης is from ταναός ‘stretched, long’ and ἀκή ‘point, edge’, and χαλκῷ stands for the weapon. φερέτω is the third-person imperative ‘let him carry’. δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι used as an order, ‘let him give back’. λελάχωσι is a reduplicated aorist subjunctive of λαγχάνω, here ‘give a share’, taking πυρός ‘of fire’, the funeral fire; θανόντα ‘dead’ agrees with με.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κ’ ἐγὼ τὸν ἕλω, δώῃ δέ μοι εὖχος Ἀπόλλων,
τεύχεα σύλησας οἴσω προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρήν,
καὶ κρεμόω προτὶ νηὸν Ἀπόλλωνος ἑκάτοιο,
sentences.l:
But if I take him, and Apollo give me a boast,
having stripped the armour I will carry it to sacred Ilium,
and hang it at the temple of Apollo the far-darter,
sentences.i: But if I kill him, and Apollo grants me the triumph, I shall strip his armour and carry it to sacred Ilium, and hang it up at the temple of Apollo the far-darter,
sentences.n: The second condition: if Hector wins, the armour goes to Apollo’s temple. εἰ δέ κ’ ἐγὼ τὸν ἕλω answers the εἰ μέν of line 77; δώῃ is the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι, ‘may he give’, and εὖχος is ‘a boast’, the claim to glory that victory gives. οἴσω is the future of φέρω; Ἴλιον ἱρήν is ‘sacred Ilium’, as at 20. κρεμόω is the epic future of κρεμάννυμι ‘hang up’, προτί the epic form of πρός, and νηόν the epic accusative of ναός ‘temple’. ἑκάτοιο is a genitive of ἕκατος, a short form whose sense alone is not certain, understood as ‘far-darter’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ νέκυν ἐπὶ νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἀποδώσω,
ὄφρά ἑ ταρχύσωσι κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί,
σῆμά τέ οἱ χεύωσιν ἐπὶ πλατεῖ Ἑλλησπόντῳ.
sentences.l:
but the corpse to the well-benched ships I will give back,
so that they may bury him, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
and heap up a tomb for him on the broad Hellespont.
sentences.i: but the corpse I will give back to the well-benched ships, so that the long-haired Achaeans may bury him and heap up a tomb for him on the broad Hellespont.
sentences.n: He promises the body back to the Achaeans for burial. τὸν δὲ νέκυν ‘but the corpse’ is set against the armour, and ἀποδώσω is the future of ἀποδίδωμι ‘give back’. ὄφρα … ταρχύσωσι ‘so that they may bury’: ταρχύω is a funeral word, ‘bury with the due rites’, whose origin is not known. ἑ is ‘him’ and οἱ ‘for him’. κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί ‘the long-haired Achaeans’ (literally ‘long-haired as to the head’) is a stock phrase. χεύωσιν is the aorist subjunctive of χέω ‘pour, heap up’, and σῆμα ‘sign, mark’ is here the grave-mound, ‘tomb’. The Hellespont is the strait beside Troy.

sentences.t:
καί ποτέ τις εἴπῃσι καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἀνθρώπων
νηῒ πολυκλήϊδι πλέων ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον·
sentences.l:
And at some time someone may say, even of men born later,
sailing in a many-thwarted ship over the wine-faced open-sea:
sentences.i: And some day someone may say, even among men born later, as he sails in a ship of many thwarts over the sea that has the look of wine:
sentences.n: Hector now pictures the fame to come. καί ποτέ τις εἴπῃσι ‘and some day someone may say’ is the form of words used at 6.459 (there with a final ν), εἴπῃσι an aorist subjunctive in the old ending -σι; καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἀνθρώπων ‘even of men born later’ says that later generations will say it. νηῒ πολυκλήϊδι is ‘a ship of many thwarts’; κληΐς is a part of a ship’s rowing gear, rendered ‘thwart’, the exact part not being certain. οἴνοπα is the accusative of οἶνοψ, from οἶνος ‘wine’ and ὄψ ‘look’: a sea ‘with the look of wine’.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρὸς μὲν τόδε σῆμα πάλαι κατατεθνηῶτος,
ὅν ποτ’ ἀριστεύοντα κατέκτανε φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l:
‘Of a man this is the tomb, who died long ago,
whom once, as he excelled, glorious Hector killed.’
sentences.i: ‘This is the tomb of a man who died long ago, whom glorious Hector once killed while he was excelling.’
sentences.n: The later sailor’s imagined words, a speech within Hector’s speech. ἀνδρὸς μὲν τόδε σῆμα ‘of a man this is the tomb’ has no verb; κατατεθνηῶτος is the genitive of the perfect participle of καταθνήσκω, ‘dead’, with πάλαι ‘long ago’. ὅν ποτ’ ἀριστεύοντα ‘whom once, as he excelled’: ἀριστεύω is ‘be the best, be a champion’, the verb from ἄριστος, and κατέκτανε is the aorist of κατακτείνω ‘kill’. The dead man is the Achaean Hector expects to kill; Hector, imagining the sailor’s words, makes him name Hector as the killer. φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t: ὥς ποτέ τις ἐρέει·
sentences.l: So at some time someone will say;
sentences.i: So someone will say some day;
sentences.n: The sailor’s words end. ὥς ‘so’ looks back to what Hector has just put in the sailor’s mouth, ποτέ τις ‘some day someone’ is as at 87, and ἐρέει is the epic future of ἐρέω ‘will say’ (Attic ἐρεῖ). The ano teleia closes the imagined words and turns back to Hector’s own.

sentences.t: τὸ δ’ ἐμὸν κλέος οὔ ποτ’ ὀλεῖται.
sentences.l: and my fame never will perish.”
sentences.i: and my fame will never perish.”
sentences.n: Hector’s hope. τὸ δ’ ἐμὸν κλέος ‘and my glory’: after the sailor’s words, Hector says what they will win for him, and δέ is only a mild ‘and’. κλέος ‘fame’ is what is heard of a man, and the phrase κλέος οὔ ποτ’ ὀλεῖται is the one at 2.325, with the same English. οὔ ποτ’ ὀλεῖται ‘will never perish’, with ὀλεῖται the future of ὄλλυμι in its middle sense. His speech ends here.
